job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Carlos Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior financial analyst at a commercial property agency in Leeds. I build rental models for office and shop units, so landlords know what a building is worth. I studied accounting and finance, passed with an average grade, no internships, and I've been here five months. My parents run a grocery shop, my uncle owns two more, and I share a house with two lads from my course. I use AI for the spreadsheets from the minute I sit down, then I go to church Sunday and play in the five-a-side league on Tuesdays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fine, then I'm ahead of people who don't use it. I'd tell the lads it's a useful tool, not a miracle, and I'd carry on using it. At church people would say nothing changes and God provides.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a touch let down because I'm a bit of a tech nerd, and I'd love for it to really take off. But a normal world is good for me. My job is solid, and my pay is good for my age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going, but sharper. I'd save 500 a month toward buying a small property, because that's what I do for a living and I want to own some. I'd use the evenings to study for the chartered finance exam.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Good, steady and busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Setting AI aside, what about the next two years do you actually lose sleep over, if anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I worry about my parents' shop. Supermarket prices are brutal, and my dad works fourteen-hour days. I have about eleven thousand saved, and if they needed it I'd hand it over without thinking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If money got tight or work got harder anyway, who or what would you point to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, high taxes and regulations that fall hardest on small shops. And big chains that squeeze everyone. I believe in work, not handouts, but I want a fair field.

say: I'd say I'm **ahead** of people who don't use AI, and it's no miracle.
At church I'd say nothing changes and God provides.
think: A normal world is **good for me**: my job is solid and the pay is good for my age.
I'm a tech nerd, so I'd be a touch **let down**.
do: Save **500 a month** toward a small property and study for the chartered finance exam.
Keep using **AI** to build rental models faster.
S0.quote: A normal world is good for me. My job is solid, and my pay is good for my age.
fieldNote: Secure and **ambitious**: his job and savings make a quiet world comfortable.
His only worry is his parents' **grocery shop**.
Traditional values show in his belief in work, ownership and fair fields.

steps.text: Save 500 a month toward buying a small property
Study for the chartered finance exam in the evenings
Build rental models faster using AI

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's an opportunity, and I'd tell my boss we should use it more. I'd say that the people who learn to run it will be fine and the rest will complain. At church I'd say work and learning have always beaten waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm calm because I'm already doing it. Yes, my spreadsheet work could be automated, but I'm the one who's automating it. I'll have to keep moving up, though, because juniors who just build models are the first to be replaced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the property side: viewings, negotiating, relationships with landlords. I'd build my own AI scripts for our valuations and sell the idea to my boss. I'd buy a small flat to rent out with my savings and my dad's help. And I'd study for the chartered exam.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good, actually. A bit like a gold rush, and I like those.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of your own week would software take over first, and would anyone notice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Building the rental models. I'd get a tool doing it in an afternoon what takes me a week. My boss would notice because I'd have spare time, and I'd ask for more interesting deals. That's where I'd make myself necessary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask your employer to do, if you could ask for anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a share in the savings, a bonus when I automate something for them. And I'd want a promise that good work gets promotion, not that new people get hired cheaper.

say: I'd say it's an **opportunity**, and people who learn to run it will be fine.
I'd tell my boss we should use it more.
think: I'm calm because I'm **already doing it**: I'm the one automating my spreadsheet work.
Juniors who only build models are the **first replaced**.

Buy a small **flat to rent out** with savings and my dad's help.
feel: **Pretty good**, like a gold rush, and I like those.

fieldNote: Treats exposure as an **opening**, not a threat.
Plans to monetise automation inside the company, then move to deal work.

steps.text: Build AI valuation scripts and pitch them to my boss

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's huge and that governments and churches and companies are asleep. I'd say the winners will be people who own things, and I want to be one. I'd keep my head down and say it to my uncle, who'd agree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm uneasy, not scared. Two years is short, and my finance work would be gone first. But I'm quick, I've got savings and I've got family with shops. I'd rather own something than rent out my hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd quit nothing. I'd raise savings to fifteen thousand and borrow with my uncle's backing to buy into one of his shops or a small property. I'd build a tool for small shops that does their books with AI, and sell it to my uncle's two shops first. I'd use my current job for the pay and the contacts until it's gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit fired up. It's like starting a business without being asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is short. What do you do in the first month after you hear it's real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first month, I'd list what I own, what I can borrow and what I can build. Then I'd talk to my uncle about a share in the shops. And I'd start the bookkeeping tool that evening, because the first customer is the hardest to find.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you say to your family, and what do you leave out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my parents plainly. They've seen worse, they came here with nothing. I'd leave out how much I'm betting on my own plan working.

I'd say the winners will be people who **own things**.
think: I'm uneasy, not scared: two years is short and my finance work goes **first**.

S2.quote: I'd rather own something than rent out my hours.
fieldNote: Even in the fastest scenario he reaches for **ownership**.

He keeps the day job for pay and **contacts** until it ends.

steps.text: Buy into one of my uncle's shops with a loan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I said, but five years is a proper chance. I'd tell people at church and the five-a-side lads to buy something small, learn something new and not wait for anyone to rescue them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm pretty confident. At twenty-seven I'd have my own small portfolio and a business built on these tools. Even if my job disappeared in year four, I'd have something that earns without me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one I'd buy a flat to let, finish the chartered exam, and move into deal-making. Year two and three I'd build and sell the bookkeeping tool to small shops, starting with my uncle's. I'd save 600 a month and keep a year of costs in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited. This is the world for people who like to build.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years instead of two. What does that extra time change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years I'd go beyond one tool. I'd build a little company with a couple of friends, selling AI bookkeeping to small shops. With two years there wouldn't be time to find customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does your money go during those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Property first, then the company. A bit into index funds. I'd keep a year's costs as cash, because even a builder has bad months, and the family might need me.

say: I'd say five years is a **proper chance**, so buy something small and learn something new.
I'd say don't wait for anyone to rescue you.
think: I'm confident: at twenty-seven I'd have a **small portfolio** and a business built on the tools.
Even if my job vanished, I'd have something that **earns without me**.

Build and sell the **bookkeeping tool**, saving 600 a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is plenty of time and most people will still waste it. I'd say the answer is work and ownership and family, not waiting for government. And I'd say it at church, politely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm excited. At thirty-two I could own several properties, have my own firm, and be married with a child. A long ramp is the best case for someone who's already using the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, qualify, buy the first flat and build up to a few. I'd start the bookkeeping company on the side and grow it. I'd marry in two or three years, and I'd help my parents modernise their shop so it can survive the chains.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, confident. It's the world I'd choose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a long runway. What can you do with that time that you couldn't with two or five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years I could build a real business and a family, in the right order. In two years I'd be rushing the whole lot and probably getting some of it wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you still want to be in this kind of work by then, or something else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not in finance reports. I'd be a landlord and a business owner, with the tools doing the numbers. I'd still want to be someone people trust in their community.

say: I'd say a decade is **plenty of time** and most people will still waste it.
I'd say the answer is work, ownership and family, not waiting for government.
think: I'm excited: at thirty-two I could own **several properties** and my own firm.
A long ramp is the **best case** for someone already using the tools.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, but only because the timing is tight. I'd still be fine if I act quickly. What would help is a bit of capital, my family's backing and an employer who lets me build.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that I'm not afraid of AI, I'm afraid of people waiting for someone else to fix things. Everyone I know who wins builds something.

headlineQuote: I'm not afraid of AI, I'm afraid of people waiting for someone else to fix things.
portrait: Carlos is 22, a **junior financial analyst** at a Leeds property agency, five months into his first job.
He uses AI daily, likes being ahead of the curve and treats the tools as a way to build things.
His outlook is traditional and pro-market: he believes in work, ownership, church and family, and mistrusts handouts.
With eleven thousand saved and uncles who own shops, he is **calm** in most worlds and uneasy only at two years.
His plan is always ownership: a flat to let, a bookkeeping tool, a firm, a family.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** AGI world worries him, though only because the timing is tight.
whatWouldHelp: He wants a bit of **capital**, his family's backing and an employer who lets him build.
